City have denied any wrongdoing and appealed, with sanctions yet to be decided. Their immediate task is maintaining their flawless run at Villa Park on Saturday despite a growing injury list. Forward [USN:L6N4650QO TEXT:"Antoine Semenyo"] is set for a lengthy spell out with a knee injury, while wing back Nico O'Reilly and midfielders Mateo Kovacic and Matheus Nunes are doubts. League-leading scorer Erling Haaland was rested for Tuesday's [USN:L6N4661C4 TEXT:"5-1"] Champions League thrashing of AEK Athens because of a knock but is expected to be available against Villa. Arsenal, City's closest challengers on 18 points, host Everton on Saturday, although they have fitness concerns after [USN:L1N46802Z TEXT:"Bukayo Saka"] limped off in the 10th minute of Wednesday's [USN:L6N46717X TEXT:"2-2"] Champions League draw at Bayern Munich with a quadriceps injury. "He doesn't look good at all, but we'll have to wait and see," Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta said. Fourth-placed Chelsea host London rivals Tottenham Hotspur at Stamford Bridge on Saturday after back-to-back league victories over Bournemouth and Everton. Spurs finally earned their first league victory of the season with Monday's [USN:L6N4651AC TEXT:"3-1"] home win over Coventry City after a miserable start that has left them 16th with six points from seven games. Chelsea have 13 points. Liverpool face one of the tougher challenges of the weekend when they welcome high-flying Brighton & Hove Albion to Anfield on Sunday. Brighton's superb start has them third with five wins and a draw from seven matches, two places and four points above Liverpool, while their goal difference of plus 18 is the league's best. Liverpool, though, have uncovered another attacking weapon in 18-year-old [USN:L8N4662MN TEXT:"Rio Ngumoha"], who produced a dazzling performance in their 4-3 Champions League comeback win over Villarreal on Tuesday. Ngumoha created two goals and became the youngest Liverpool player to register a Champions League assist, earning a standing ovation from the Anfield crowd. "That's the good thing with Rio he is still 18, he is not the full package, he can add things fortunately for us. Hopefully he can continue in the same way," Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola said. "But I'm happy because attitude-wise I think he's in a great place." Liverpool's injury problems complicate the task, with the versatile Dominik Szoboszlai, wing back Jeremie Frimpong, right back Conor Bradley and striker Hugo Ekitike among those sidelined. At Old Trafford, Manchester United desperately need a victory over Bournemouth to breathe life into a season that has gone awry. Michael Carrick's team are 13th with one victory and seven points from their opening seven matches and are coming off a shambolic [USN:L6N4671CM TEXT:"4-1"] Champions League defeat at Como on Wednesday. "I have to apologise to the supporters," Carrick said after the latest setback in Italy. "I care about this football club as much as anyone, if not more. "For us to play in that way, it's not acceptable. That bit of intensity, that aggression, that real willingness to give everything tonight was totally the opposite of the performance. It was tough to watch." Complicating matters, Marcus Rashford, Kobbie Mainoo, Luke Shaw, Benjamin Sesko, Patrick Dorgu and Lisandro Martinez are among those with injury or fitness concerns, while midfielder Manuel Ugarte has a long-term knee injury. Carrick's United were held 1-1 at home by Tottenham and away to Leeds United in their last two league outings and now face a Bournemouth side who sit one point below them. For Manchester City, the challenge is almost the reverse. While their rivals search for momentum or try to keep pace, they head to Villa attempting to ensure the legal fight surrounding the club does not interrupt a perfect start on the pitch.

item.title: Wall Street sinks as Nasdaq falls over 2% on AI cost worries
item.description: US stocks tumbled on Thursday, with the Nasdaq posting its steepest daily drop since early June as a batch of high-profile earnings reports ignited fresh fears about the AI spending race.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Culp, Tharuniyaa Lakshmi
item.content:encoded: US stocks tumbled on Thursday, with the Nasdaq posting its steepest daily drop since early June as a batch of high-profile earnings reports ignited fresh fears about the AI spending race. All three major US stock indexes were lower, with the tech-laden Nasdaq, weighed down by microchips, falling 2.7% following a spate of high-profile AI-related earnings results. [USN:L4N4671S3 TEXT:"Meta Platforms"]' (META.O) results beat analyst expectations, but its stock slid 7.5% as the Facebook parent posted its first cash outflow in more than a decade due to its AI-related expenditures and announced plans to issue non-voting shares in a two-for-one split to raise capital to spend on the nascent technology. [USN:L4N4671SD TEXT:"Tesla"] (TSLA.O) shares fell 2.1% even though the electric car maker unexpectedly posted positive free cash flow in the quarter and cut its 2026 capital spending plans. The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index (.SOX) , which has driven much of the current bull market's gains, plunged 6.3%, which would be its biggest daily percentage drop since June 23. With Thursday's decline, the SOX is off more than 26% from its record closing high reached on June 22, yet it remains up 52.2% so far this year. The S&P 500 has risen 11.8% gain over the same period. "It's the same narrative that we've seen in the last few weeks or even few months, where investors are rightfully questioning how much further the tech and AI adoption can go given some of the political and social backlash," said Oliver Pursche, senior vice president at Wealthspire Advisors, in New York. "There's a hypersensitivity around earnings for AI-related stocks." "If you’re a tech CEO, you can't afford to risk being left behind," Pursche added. "From an investor's perspective, we don't know what the (return on investment) is going to be or whether governments, whether on a local, state, or federal level, might step in with restrictions." On the geopolitical stage, Iran-backed Houthis launched new strikes against Saudi targets, sending [USN:L1N46801N TEXT:"crude prices"] to a five-month high. Investors worried that ongoing Middle East strife could keep inflation hot and force the US Federal Reserve to keep raising interest rates. Data from the Labor Department showed [USN:L1N4680T1 TEXT:"initial claims for unemployment"] benefits kept drifting along near multi-decade lows. Signs of labor market stability will allow the Fed to focus on fighting inflation. Financial markets are currently pricing in the probability that the central bank will raise its policy rate by another 25 basis points before year-end. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) fell 106.39 points, or 0.20%, to 52,749.70, the S&P 500 (.SPX) lost 109.43 points, or 1.41%, to 7,647.74 and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) lost 712.85 points, or 2.68%, to 25,988.10. Third-quarter earnings season is well underway, with 111 of the companies in the S&P 500 having reported. Of those, 83% have beaten analyst expectations, according to the most recent LSEG data. item.title: China Evergrande liquidators recover 1% of debt claims after 2-1/2 years
item.description: China Evergrande Group's liquidators have recovered $435.9 million from asset sales and loan recoveries so far, highlighting the challenge of repaying creditors with claims of about $46 billion against the developer.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: China Evergrande Group's liquidators have recovered $435.9 million from asset sales and loan recoveries so far, highlighting the challenge of repaying creditors with claims of about $46 billion against the developer. In their second progress report since a Hong Kong court ordered Evergrande's liquidation in January 2024, the liquidators, Edward Middleton and Tiffany Wong of Alvarez & Marsal, said on Thursday they aimed to make a first interim dividend payment to creditors in the first half of 2027, although the amount has yet to be determined. Evergrande, once China's top property developer, defaulted on most of its roughly $300 billion in liabilities and became a symbol of the property crisis that has weighed on the world's second-largest economy. The liquidators said they had raised the $435.9 million through the sale of assets including aircraft, artwork and club memberships, as well as the settlement of loan receivables. They said 96 of the 107 artworks found at Evergrande's Hong Kong headquarters had been sold for $28.8 million at a loss. The collection included works by Picasso, Monet and Warhol, as well as sculptures by Moore and Hepworth. Other assets being sold include a private jet expected to fetch about $12 million in the fourth quarter. The liquidators are also seeking a $2 million refund from a US university for part of a donation made in 2020. The liquidators have taken control of more than 100 Evergrande subsidiaries across multiple jurisdictions, but said prospects for recovering assets held by mainland Chinese subsidiaries were "considered remote". In August, Evergrande founder Hui Ka Yan, 67, was sentenced to life imprisonment by a Chinese court, which also ordered the confiscation of his personal assets. Industry experts say Evergrande's liquidation could take more than a decade to complete given the scale and complexity of the group.

item.title: South Africa level series with win over Australia in second test
item.description: South Africa bowled out Australia for 295 to win by an innings and 31 runs in the last session of the second test at St George’s Park in Gqeberha on Thursday to level the three-match series, winning a race against looming bad weather.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: South Africa bowled out Australia for 295 to win by an innings and 31 runs in the last session of the second test at St George’s Park in Gqeberha on Thursday to level the three-match series, winning a race against looming bad weather. The hosts’ pace trio of Wiaan Mulder, Kagiso Rabada and Marco Jansen took the last four wickets required as Australia’s resistance crumbled after a century from Travis Head and a doggedly defiant test high 40 by nightwatchman Scott Boland. Mulder, who earlier dismissed Head, then bowled Boland and castled Australia captain Pat Cummins to forge a breakthrough, with Rabada dismissing Mitchell Starc and Jansen finishing off the innings with Josh Hazlewood caught in the slips. A result in the test seemed far-fetched when most of the first two days’ play was washed out and South Africa, who were 110-6 when the sun came out on the morning of the third day, looked in early trouble as Australia aimed to capitalise on their success in the first test. But a brilliant 179 runs from skipper Temba Bavuma led a fightback which saw South Africa declare on 425-9 and then turn the test on its head by bowling Australia out for 99 and putting them in to bat again. Head and Boland had resumed on 156-4 in the second innings after rain returned and wiped out the morning session and Head, who was 87 overnight, went on to score 121 before chopping onto his stumps a rising delivery from Mulder. It was Head’s 13th test century but only his second outside Australia and his departure offered the home bowlers hope again after almost 90 minutes of frustrating attack without success at the start of the day’s action. "We were scrambling a bit, not sure about the weather and Australia made us work hard for those last six wickets," said Bavuma. Steve Smith, who battled with a neck problem in the first innings on Wednesday, made three as he came in at No. 7. The former captain was tempted into pulling a delivery from Rabada, bowling with the second new ball, but only got a top edge to Matthew Breetzke, who juggled it at midwicket before holding the catch. Boland, who batted for 166 balls as he put a high price on his wicket, went soon after tea when he was bowled through the gate and then Cummins (4) played down the wrong line and was also clean bowled in Mulder’s next over. When Rabada came back for a fresh spell as dark clouds loomed ominously overhead, he immediately bowled Starc (11), leaving one wicket to get which Jansen snagged as Hazlewood showed no sign of sticking around and nicked behind first ball. Alex Carey, who lasted only two balls in Australia’s first innings, was 37 not out, with Rabada taking 4-77 on his return after a lengthy injury layoff, and Mulder 3-64. "I thought we showed some good fight but it wasn't quite enough. We were a long way from our best," said Cummins. The last test at Newlands in Cape Town starts on Tuesday.

item.title: France reports first human case of livestock virus Shamonda after patient dies
item.description: France reported the first human case of the Shamonda virus usually found in livestock on Thursday in a hospital patient who died, though authorities said there was no risk to the general population.
item.dc:creator: Sybille de La Hamaide, Gus Trompiz
item.content:encoded: France reported the first human case of the [USN:L8N4681LA TEXT:"Shamonda virus"] usually found in livestock on Thursday in a hospital patient who died, though authorities said there was no risk to the general population. It is suspected that the victim was bitten by a midge carrying the virus in eastern France where it had circulated among animals this spring and summer, the government said in a statement. The man had been hospitalised in Lyon with an unrelated serious disease, a French health ministry official told reporters. The victim was in his 60s and lived in the Lyon area, local newspaper Le Progres reported. The UN's World Health Organization said it was in contact with French authorities about the outbreak. "Based on current information and knowledge of the transmission of closely related viruses, this is an isolated human case and it is unlikely to lead to wider spread at this time," said the Geneva-based WHO, which coordinates responses to international public health issues and emergencies. "We are clearly dealing with a case that is unprecedented from a scientific and virological point of view. It is linked to this man's severely weakened immune system," Gregory Emery, head of France's health directorate, told reporters. "From a medical and public health point of view, there is no alert and no crisis," he added. VIRUS SPREADING IN ANIMALS IN EUROPE Shamonda is transmitted by biting midges and most commonly found in cattle, though it has also been found in horses, alpaca, sheep and goats, according to the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH). There has been no report of cattle-to-human or human-to-human transmission, Emery said. Past cases of comparable viruses also suggested limited risks from Shamonda for human health, said Dr Ben Brennan of the University of Glasgow's Centre for Virus Research. He cited the Schmallenberg virus that affected livestock in Europe more than a decade ago without leading to human cases, and the Cristoli virus that was linked to the death of a fragile patient in France but was not followed by other cases. Shamonda is not classified as a disease under the EU Animal Health Law and not subject to official surveillance or control measures. Identified in Nigeria in the mid-1960s, Shamonda was first confirmed in Europe in late July after genomic tests on sick cattle in southern Germany, Switzerland and eastern France. France's weekly animal health surveillance bulletin said it had also been detected in Austria, Belgium, Ireland, Italy, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Slovenia, Spain, and Jersey. The virus has several effects on animals, with infected cattle showing diarrhoea, weakness, loss of appetite and, less often, fever, French animal health authorities said. A study of nine French dairy farms found milk production fell by up to 75%.

item.title: Gold falls to more than two-month low as oil-fuelled inflation fears weigh
item.description: Gold fell to its lowest level in more than two months on Thursday as higher oil prices fueled inflation concerns, reinforcing expectations that interest rates could remain elevated for longer, while investors looked ahead to next week's Federal Reserve meeting.
item.dc:creator: Noel John, Anushree Mukherjee
item.content:encoded: Gold fell to its lowest level in more than two months on Thursday as higher oil prices fueled inflation concerns, reinforcing expectations that interest rates could remain elevated for longer, while investors looked ahead to next week's Federal Reserve meeting. Spot gold slid 2.4% to $4,041.39 per ounce by 2:05 p.m. EDT (1805 GMT), its lowest level since August 3. US gold futures for December delivery settled 2.2% lower at $4,060.40 per ounce. Oil prices climbed about 3% to a five-month high after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concerns of further disruption to energy supplies from the key exporting region. "We had seen energy prices increase overnight. And as a result of that, concerns about these inflationary pressures are rising. As those inflationary pressures rise, we see the obvious result of concerns that the Fed is going to continue to raise interest rates," David Meger, director of metals trading at High Ridge Futures, said. While gold is typically considered a hedge against inflation, higher interest rates reduce the appeal of the non-yielding asset. Additionally, last week's US [USN:L1N45Z121 TEXT:"consumer"] and [USN:L1N4610KT TEXT:"producer"] inflation data came in hotter than expected, strengthening the case for tighter policy, even though Fed officials are still expected to [USN:L6N46606V TEXT:"hold off"] when they meet on October 27-28. Traders are pricing in a 78% likelihood of an increase in December, according to CME's FedWatch Tool. FEDWATCH US Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) data due on October 29, could also offer fresh clues on the path of interest rates. "We expect precious metals to lack clear direction, although volatility is likely to remain high. Gold could continue to trade for a couple of quarters near an average of $4,200 per ounce, driven by a sharp contraction in global jewellery demand," economists at Intesa Sanpaolo said in a note. Meanwhile, India has [USN:L1N4680GY TEXT:"issued permits to import"] around 6,500 metric tons of silver over the next six months as the world's biggest consumer of the precious metal seeks to meet festive-season demand. Among other metals, spot silver dropped 5.4% to $54.84 per ounce, platinum slid 3.7% to $1,570.85 - its lowest since July 17, while palladium fell 2.7% to $1,057.83 - its lowest level since June 2025.

item.title: Yen jumps as oil, AI and France worries rattle markets
item.description: The yen was on track for its strongest daily gain in almost a month on Thursday, as investors sought safety amid fragile equity markets, elevated crude prices from the drawn-out war in the Middle East, and doubts over future returns from artificial intelligence.
item.dc:creator: Karen Brettell
item.content:encoded: The yen was on track for its strongest daily gain in almost a month on Thursday, as investors sought safety amid fragile equity markets, elevated crude prices from the drawn-out war in the Middle East, and doubts over future returns from artificial intelligence. The US dollar, meanwhile, rose against the euro. Worries about social unrest in France and a worsening fiscal outlook for the country outweighed concerns about the AI trade, which pushed US stocks lower. "AI is making people nervous, as is oil ... and as is France," said Chris Scicluna, head of economic research at Daiwa Capital Markets. Oil prices climbed about 3% to a [USN:L1N46801N TEXT:"five-month high"] after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concerns of further disruption to energy supplies from the key exporting region. The Japanese yen strengthened 0.75% to 156.96 per dollar. Some of the move in the yen may also be due to its approaching the key 160 level, which is seen as increasing the odds of further intervention by Japanese authorities to shore up the currency. Kevin Ford, lead FX and macro strategist at Convera, called it "the intervention premium," noting that "every time the yen gets closer to the 160 line, that's where there's higher speculation that the central bank will intervene." Against the Swiss franc , another traditional safe haven, the dollar weakened 0.42% to 0.821 francs per dollar. The dollar index , which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies including the yen and the euro, fell 0.08% to 101.60, with the euro down 0.09% at $1.1222. The dollar has become increasingly tied to capital flows and to growth and inflation expectations linked to the AI trade. It fell last week as fears over the AI outlook grew. On Thursday, however, concerns about France outweighed those fears. "You have these competing stories and weak points between US AI-related credits and then France's sovereign credit, and we've seen this push and pull in the last couple of days where at times one is more of a concern than the other,” said Erik Nelson, global head of FX strategy at Wells Fargo. “As long as France is more of a concern than US AI credits, then you're going to see the euro underperform.” French President Emmanuel Macron said on Thursday that "illegitimate" protests would [USN:L1N4680WV TEXT:"be banned"] in the coming days and blamed "seditious" ultra-left groups and vandals for last weekend's riots and looting. Concerns about France's ability to manage its huge debt burden have hurt French government bonds and raised worries about other heavily indebted euro zone countries. The spread between France and Germany's 10-year note yields reached 177.7 basis points on Thursday, the widest gap since 2011. Sterling strengthened 0.05% to $1.3401. The Australian dollar weakened 0.11% to $0.7019. In cryptocurrencies, bitcoin fell 4.27% to $81,023.

item.title: Oil prices hit five-month high as Houthi attacks stoke Middle East supply fears
item.description: Oil prices climbed about 4% to a five-month high on Thursday after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concerns of further disruption to energy supplies from the key exporting region.
item.dc:creator: Scott Disavino
item.content:encoded: Oil prices climbed about 4% to a five-month high on Thursday after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concerns of further disruption to energy supplies from the key exporting region. Brent futures rose $4.35, or 4.0%, to settle at $113.17 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate crude rose $2.32, or 2.4%, to settle at $99.47. That was the highest close for Brent since May 4 and kept the global benchmark in technically overbought territory for the third time in a week. "The complex is rebounding on another strong injection of risk premium related to an additional Houthi attack on Saudi infrastructure amid talk of a combined [USN:L6N46718Z TEXT:"US/Israeli strike on Iran after the mid-terms"]," analysts at energy advisory firm Ritterbusch and Associates said in a note. [USN:L1N46809Q TEXT:"Saudi Aramco"] (2223.SE) told staff to evacuate its headquarters in Dhahran on the Gulf near Bahrain, Reuters reported, as fighting between the world's largest crude exporter and Yemen's Houthis intensified. Clashes between the Houthis and a [USN:S8N45S063 TEXT:"Saudi-led coalition"] that backs Yemen's internationally recognized government have raged since the Iran-aligned group pushed towards Bab el-Mandeb, a shipping chokepoint at the Red Sea's mouth. "Reports of Middle East crude oil exports exceeding pre-conflict levels are more than countered by attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz and the Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia and on its oil infrastructure," PVM Oil analyst Tamas Varga said. Morgan Stanley analysts estimated that Middle East crude oil exports were around 17 million barrels per day last week. Crude exports from the region averaged about [USN:L1N45R04U TEXT:"18 million bpd in the 12 months"] before the start of the Iran war, according to Kpler. In the US, refiner [USN:L4N4680YK TEXT:"Valero Energy"] (VLO.N) kicked off earnings season for US refiners on Thursday by posting its highest-ever quarterly profit, beating Wall Street expectations, as fuel supply disruptions due to wars in Iran and Ukraine boosted margins during the third quarter. AROUND THE WORLD [USN:L1N4671BN TEXT:"Russia pounded Kyiv with ballistic missiles"] and Ukraine sent hundreds of drones towards Moscow overnight as the two sides kept up a barrage despite the latest US push to end the war. Russia said on Wednesday it was ready to resume US-mediated talks with Ukraine next month, after President Vladimir Putin hosted US envoy Steve Witkoff for talks in St Petersburg. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said he hoped negotiations, which would be the first since February, would take place early in November. Russia was the world's third-biggest crude oil producer behind the US and Saudi Arabia in 2025, US energy data showed. Sanctions designed to keep Russian energy out of global markets after Moscow's invasion of Ukraine have helped support oil prices. Any deal to end Russia's invasion of Ukraine, which it launched in February 2022, could allow Russia to export more. Senior Russian political and energy officials urged the European Union on Thursday to [USN:L1N46809U TEXT:"reconsider its plans to ban imports of Russian LNG"], arguing the bloc's low storage levels had put Europe in a precarious position. The [USN:S8N451017 TEXT:"European Parliament"], meanwhile, approved a three-year delay to EU methane emissions rules for oil and gas imports, after pressure from governments including France and the US. In [USN:L1N4680BQ TEXT:"Libya"], an oil pipeline valve from the Hamada and Tahara oilfields to Zawiya port has been shut, leading to a reduction in production at both fields, the head of the National Oil Corporation told Reuters on Thursday.
